lessons.title: Why Heat Honey? Pros and Cons
lessons.body:
Heating honey is one of the most common steps in honey processing, but it comes with trade-offs. The main reason to heat honey is to make it easier to handle. Raw honey often crystallizes, becoming thick and grainy. Gentle heating (around 40â45Â°C) turns those crystals back into liquid, so you can strain, bottle, and sell it smoothly. Heating also helps remove air bubbles, which makes the honey look clearer and more attractive on the shelf. Another reason is to kill yeast cells that cause fermentation. If honey has too much moisture (above 18â20%), wild yeasts can make it ferment, spoiling the batch. Pasteurization (heating to 60â70Â°C for a short time) kills most yeasts and molds, giving a longer shelf life. In hot African climates, where storage temperatures can exceed 30Â°C, this is a real concern.

However, heating honey has downsides. High heat destroys beneficial enzymes like diastase and invertase, and it reduces antioxidants and aroma compounds. Overheating above 70Â°C can create a burnt, caramel-like taste and darken the honey. It also produces a chemical called hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), which in large amounts is a quality issue and can be harmful. Raw honey advocates argue that unheated honey retains more health benefits, and many customers in Africa and abroad pay a premium for raw honey. So you must balance the practical need for liquid, stable honey against the loss of natural qualities.

For small-scale processors in Africa, the choice depends on your market. If you sell to local customers who value raw honey, you might skip heating or only warm gently to decrystallize. If you supply supermarkets or export, pasteurization may be required for consistency and shelf life. In either case, use the lowest temperature that does the job, and never boil honey. A simple thermometer is your best tool. Remember that heating is not always necessary: good harvesting and storage at cool temperatures can keep honey liquid and stable without any heat.

lessons.title: Pasteurization Temperatures and Times
lessons.body:
Pasteurization is the process of heating honey to kill yeast and other microorganisms, then cooling it quickly. The goal is to make honey shelf-stable without cooking it. For honey, the standard pasteurization temperature is 60â70Â°C (140â158Â°F). At 60Â°C, you need to hold the honey for about 30 minutes. At 70Â°C, you only need about 2â5 minutes. Many small processors use 65Â°C for 15â20 minutes as a practical middle ground. These combinations kill most yeast cells while minimizing damage to enzymes and flavor. Never go above 80Â°C, as that causes rapid quality loss and HMF formation.

To pasteurize, you need a stainless steel pot, a thermometer that reads up to 100Â°C, and a heat source you can control. A gas cooker or charcoal stove with a diffuser works, but you must stir constantly to avoid hot spots. Use a double boiler (a smaller pot inside a larger pot of boiling water) for gentler, more even heat. For larger batches, a water bath or a jacketed kettle is ideal. Measure the honey's temperature, not the water's. Once the honey reaches the target temperature, start your timer. Keep stirring slowly to distribute heat evenly.

After the hold time, cool the honey as quickly as possible. Place the pot in a cold water bath, or use a cooling coil. Rapid cooling from 65Â°C to below 40Â°C within 10â15 minutes helps prevent further heat damage and stops the cooking process. Then let it settle, skim off any foam, and bottle. Always test your process with a small batch first. Record the temperature and time for each batch, so you can repeat good results. In Africa, where ambient temperatures are high, you may need to cool the honey even faster to avoid slow cooling that continues to degrade quality. A clean, well-controlled pasteurization can extend shelf life to 2 years or more without refrigeration.

lessons.title: Using a Double Boiler for Small Batches
lessons.body:
A double boiler is the safest way to heat honey in small batches, especially if you are processing 5â20 kg at a time. It consists of two pots: a larger bottom pot filled with water, and a smaller top pot that holds the honey. The water boils, and the steam gently heats the honey without direct flame. This prevents scorching and gives you precise control. You can make a simple double boiler using two cooking pots that stack, or buy a stainless steel double boiler. Avoid aluminium pots, as honey is acidic and can react with the metal, giving a metallic taste.

To set up, fill the bottom pot with water about one-third full. Put the top pot with honey inside, making sure the bottom of the top pot does not touch the boiling water. The steam does the heating. Heat the water to a rolling boil, then reduce to a simmer. Stir the honey every few minutes with a clean, dry wooden or stainless steel spoon. Use a thermometer to monitor the honey temperature. For decrystallization, aim for 40â45Â°C. For pasteurization, bring it to 60â70Â°C and hold for the required time. The double boiler heats slowly, so allow 20â30 minutes for a 10 kg batch to reach 65Â°C.

Never leave the honey unattended. If the water in the bottom pot boils dry, the top pot can overheat quickly. Check the water level every 10 minutes and add more hot water if needed. Also, avoid getting water into the honeyâeven a few drops can increase moisture content and cause fermentation. Keep a lid on the top pot when not stirring to prevent steam condensation from dripping in. After heating, remove the top pot and cool the honey in a cold water bath. Clean your double boiler thoroughly after each use. For African beekeepers with limited equipment, a double boiler made from two large saucepans is affordable and effective. It is slower than direct heating, but it protects the honey's quality and your investment.

lessons.title: Avoiding Overheating and Caramelization
lessons.body:
Overheating honey is one of the most common mistakes in small-scale processing. When honey is heated above 70Â°C, the sugars begin to caramelize, giving a burnt, bitter taste and a dark brown color. This is irreversible and ruins the honey's value. At 80Â°C, damage happens quicklyâwithin minutes. The key is to never let honey exceed 70Â°C, and to use the lowest temperature that achieves your goal. For simple decrystallization, 40â45Â°C is enough. For pasteurization, 60â65Â°C is safer than 70Â°C. Always use a thermometer; do not rely on guesswork or visual cues.

Signs of overheating include a strong cooked or caramel smell, a darker color than the original, and a bitter aftertaste. You might also see bubbles forming rapidly and a lot of foam. If you catch it early, you can stop heating and cool immediately, but some damage may already be done. To prevent overheating, use a double boiler or a water bath, stir constantly, and never leave the pot unattended. Also, avoid heating honey in a microwave, as it heats unevenly and can create hot spots that burn the honey. In Africa, where many processors use open fires, a simple heat diffuser (a metal plate between the fire and the pot) can help distribute heat and prevent scorching.

Another cause of overheating is trying to heat too much honey at once. Large batches take longer and may develop hot spots at the bottom. Process in smaller batches, no more than 20 kg per pot, and stir frequently. If you must heat a large volume, use a jacketed kettle or a water bath with constant stirring. Remember that honey is a poor conductor of heat, so the bottom can be much hotter than the top. A thermometer placed only at the top will not show the true temperature. Stir well before checking. Finally, if you accidentally overheat a batch, do not mix it with good honey. Sell it as a lower-grade product or use it for baking, but never pass it off as premium honey.

lessons.title: Cooling and Handling After Heating
lessons.body:
Cooling is just as important as heating. After pasteurization or decrystallization, honey must be cooled quickly to stop the cooking process and prevent further quality loss. The target is to bring the honey from 60â70Â°C down to below 40Â°C within 10â15 minutes. Slow cooling allows the honey to stay hot for longer, increasing HMF levels and destroying more enzymes. In hot African climates, where the air temperature might be 35Â°C, passive cooling is too slow. You need active cooling.

The simplest method is a cold water bath. Fill a large basin or sink with cold water and ice if available. Place the pot of hot honey into the water, making sure water does not get into the honey. Stir the honey gently and occasionally stir the water around the pot to carry heat away. Change the water if it becomes warm. For a 10 kg batch, this can cool the honey to 40Â°C in about 10â15 minutes. If you have a cooling coil (a stainless steel tube through which cold water flows), you can immerse it in the honey for faster cooling. Another option is to pour the honey into shallow trays, which increases the surface area and speeds cooling. But be careful: hot honey is less viscous and easier to handle, but it can also splash and burn you.

After cooling, let the honey settle for a few hours or overnight. During this time, air bubbles rise to the top and any fine wax or debris floats. Skim off the foam with a clean spoon. Then bottle the honey into clean, dry jars. Do not bottle hot honey, as it can shrink the lids and create a weak seal, leading to leakage or spoilage. Also, hot honey can continue to cook in the jar. Once bottled, store in a cool, dark place. If you heated the honey for pasteurization, it may remain liquid for months. If you only warmed it to decrystallize, it may crystallize again over time, but that is natural. Always label your honey with the processing date and method. Good cooling and handling ensure your honey reaches the customer in top condition.

lessons.title: Alternative: Raw Honey Processing
lessons.body:
Raw honey processing means handling honey without heating it above natural hive temperature (around 35Â°C). The goal is to preserve all the natural enzymes, antioxidants, aroma, and beneficial compounds. Raw honey is increasingly popular in Africa and in export markets, where customers pay a premium for unheated, unprocessed honey. To produce raw honey, you must start with good honey: harvest only fully capped combs, which have low moisture (below 18%). If moisture is higher, raw honey may ferment. So test with a refractometer if possible; otherwise, rely on capped combs and taste.

The process is simple: crush and strain. Cut the capped combs into a clean bucket, crush them with a clean potato masher or your hands (with gloves), then let the honey drain through a sieve or cheesecloth. Do not squeeze too hard, as that can introduce wax particles. Let it drain for 24â48 hours in a warm room (25â30Â°C). Then skim off any foam and bottle. No heating is involved. You can also use a honey extractor, which spins the honey out of the comb without crushing it. That yields cleaner honey with less wax. After extraction, let the honey settle, then bottle. Raw honey may crystallize over time, which is normal and not a sign of spoilage. If you want to keep it liquid, store it at cool temperatures (below 20Â°C) or warm it very gently (below 40Â°C) just before useâbut that technically makes it no longer raw.

Raw honey processing has challenges. It requires very clean, dry equipment to avoid fermentation. It also takes longer because you cannot heat to speed up straining. And in hot climates, raw honey may ferment if moisture is too high. However, the benefits are clear: better flavor, higher nutritional value, and a premium price. For small-scale African beekeepers, raw honey is often the best choice for local markets and health-conscious customers. You can process small batches with minimal equipment: a bucket, a sieve, and clean jars. Just remember that raw honey is not sterile; it may contain yeast and spores. That is acceptable for most adults, but not for infants under one year. Always label raw honey clearly and store it properly.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Heating, Pasteurization and Raw Handling of Honey

Heating is the single most consequential decision a honey processor makes. It determines shelf life, appearance, crystallisation behaviour, export compliance and â critically â the price your product can command. For African honey businesses, from smallholder co-operatives in Tanzania and Ethiopia to commercial packers in Kenya, Nigeria and Zambia, getting heating right is the difference between a product that sells at premium retail and one that ferments, darkens or fails an export test.

This practical reference supports the module Honey Processing: Heating and Pasteurization. Use it alongside the lessons on why we heat honey, pasteurization temperatures and times, double-boiler technique, avoiding caramelization, post-heat cooling, and raw honey processing.

Key Data: Pasteurization Regimes and Their Effects

Pasteurization is not sterilization. It reduces yeast load and delays crystallisation, but honey is naturally hostile to microbial growth due to its low water activity (0.5â0.6) and high sugar content. Heating targets osmophilic yeasts (Zygosaccharomyces spp.) that cause fermentation in high-moisture honey.

Table 1: Common honey heating regimes and outcomes
Process Temperature Hold time Primary purpose Effect on quality
Warming for decrystallisation 40â45Â°C 12â24 hrs Dissolve crystals for bottling Minimal HMF increase; preserves enzymes
Liquefaction / filtration 45â50Â°C 1â4 hrs Reduce viscosity for straining Minor aroma loss
Light pasteurization 60â63Â°C 15â30 min Kill yeast; delay crystallisation Some enzyme loss; aroma reduction
Standard pasteurization 63â66Â°C 30 min Commercial shelf stability Noticeable aroma/colour change
Flash pasteurization 70â78Â°C 15â60 sec High-throughput industrial line Higher HMF; enzyme destruction
Overheating (avoid) >80Â°C any â Caramelization, HMF spike, darkening

Sources: Codex Alimentarius Standard for Honey (CODEX STAN 12-1981, rev. 2019); FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin No. 124 (1996); EU Honey Directive 2001/110/EC; Kenya Bureau of Standards KS EAS 36:2019.

Key Data: Quality Indicators After Heating

Buyers â especially EU and Middle East importers â test for hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), diastase (amylase) activity and moisture. These three numbers tell the story of how your honey was handled.

Table 2: Quality limits and commercial implications
Parameter Raw / premium Codex / EU limit Business impact if exceeded
HMF (mg/kg) <15 â¤40 (general); â¤80 tropical Rejected at EU border; downgraded to industrial grade
Diastase number (Schade) >15 â¥8 (general); â¥3 tropical Signals overheating; premium buyers reject
Moisture content <18% â¤20% Fermentation risk; short shelf life
Sucrose (apparent) <3% â¤5% (general) Suggests overfeeding of bees or adulteration
Colour (Pfund) as harvested no limit Darkening reduces value in light-honey markets

Sources: Codex Alimentarius CODEX STAN 12-1981; International Honey Commission (IHC) Harmonised Methods; EU Directive 2001/110/EC.

â  SAFETY WARNING â DO NOT HEAT HONEY DIRECTLY OVER FLAME OR IN A MICROWAVE.

Direct heat causes localised temperatures above 100Â°C, producing HMF, caramelization and potentially hazardous steam burns when honey boils. Honey also expands when heated â never fill containers more than two-thirds. Always use a water bath (double boiler) with a calibrated thermometer. In small rural processing units, keep a bucket of cool water and a fire blanket within reach. Honey at 60Â°C+ causes serious burns on skin contact â wear long sleeves, closed shoes and heat-resistant gloves.

Practical Notes for African Processors

Equipment realities. Most small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Africa do not have industrial plate heat exchangers. The double boiler â a honey pot suspended in a larger water pot â remains the workhorse. A 20-litre inner pot over a 40-litre outer pot on a gas or charcoal stove can process 15 kg of honey per batch. Add a 0â100Â°C dairy thermometer (US$3â8) and a wooden stirrer.

Energy costs. In Kenya and Nigeria, electricity tariffs and unreliable supply make gas or briquette heating more practical. A double boiler uses roughly 30â40% less fuel than direct heating because water buffers the temperature. Batch size matters: heating 15 kg takes 25â35 minutes to reach 60Â°C, then a 30-minute hold.

Water content first. Never pasteurize honey above 20% moisture â you will trap fermentation potential. Test with a refractometer (US$25â60) before heating. If moisture is high, blend with a drier batch or use a dehumidifier room rather than more heat.

Raw honey as a business model. Raw, unheated honey commands 20â40% higher prices in urban African markets (Nairobi, Lagos, Accra, Johannesburg) and in diaspora export channels. But raw honey crystallises, ferments faster and has shorter shelf life. Successful raw producers sell fast, use small batches, package in glass, and educate customers. Many processors run a dual line: pasteurized for supermarkets and bulk, raw for premium direct sales.

Cooling is part of the process. After heating, honey must cool to below 35Â°C before bottling â ideally to 25â30Â°C. Bottling hot causes condensation inside the jar, raising surface moisture and inviting fermentation. Cool in the water bath by replacing warm water with cool water, or in a shaded, dust-free room. Never cool in a refrigerator â condensation and thermal shock risk cracking glass.

Record keeping. For export or supermarket supply, keep a batch log: date, source apiary, moisture %, starting temperature, target temperature, hold time, cooling time, HMF test if available. Buyers increasingly demand traceability.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Test moisture with a refractometer before heating â reject or blend anything above 20%.
  • â Use a double boiler (water bath) â never direct flame, never microwave.
  • â Calibrate your thermometer in ice water (0Â°C) and boiling water (100Â°C) before each batch.
  • â For pasteurization, hold at 60â63Â°C for 30 minutes; never exceed 65Â°C unless flash-processing.
  • â Stir gently and continuously â avoid whipping air into the honey.
  • â Cool to below 35Â°C before bottling; check jar temperature by hand before filling.
  • â Record batch data (temperature, time, moisture, source) in a logbook for every batch.
  • â Label raw vs. pasteurized clearly â different markets, different prices, different claims.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  1. FAO â Value-Added Products from Beekeeping (Agricultural Services Bulletin No. 124) â Chapter 6 covers honey processing, heating and equipment in detail.
  2. Codex Alimentarius â Standard for Honey (CODEX STAN 12-1981) â official international quality limits including HMF and diastase.
  3. International Honey Commission (IHC) â Harmonised Methods of Honey Analysis â the reference methods used by testing labs worldwide.
  4. FAO â Beekeeping in Africa: A Manual (2012) â practical processing and marketing guidance for African contexts.
  5. Tanzania Bureau of Standards / TIC â Honey Standards and Export Guidance â example of a national standards body with free downloadable honey specifications.

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills Programme â Course: Honey Processing & Packaging. Module: Honey Processing: Heating and Pasteurization.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to heat honey?
options: A) To increase its moisture content
B) To make it easier to handle and extend shelf life
D) To make it crystallize faster
quiz.explanation: Heating decrystallizes honey and kills yeast, making it easier to bottle and giving it a longer shelf life.

quiz.q: At what temperature does honey begin to caramelize and develop off-flavors?
quiz.explanation: Overheating above 70Â°C causes caramelization, darkening, and a burnt taste.

quiz.q: What is a safe pasteurization temperature and time for honey?
quiz.explanation: 60Â°C for 30 minutes kills yeast while minimizing damage to honey quality.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for safe heating of honey?
quiz.explanation: A thermometer allows you to monitor temperature and avoid overheating.

quiz.q: What is a double boiler used for?
options: B) To heat honey gently and evenly
quiz.explanation: A double boiler uses steam to heat honey gently, preventing scorching.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid aluminium pots when heating honey?
options: B) They react with honey's acidity, causing metallic taste
D) They are not available in Africa
quiz.explanation: Honey is acidic and can react with aluminium, giving a metallic off-flavor.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after pasteurizing honey?
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling stops the cooking process and prevents further quality loss.

quiz.q: What is a sign that honey has been overheated?
options: A) It becomes lighter in color
B) It has a burnt, caramel-like smell
quiz.explanation: Overheated honey develops a burnt smell and darker color due to caramelization.

quiz.q: How can you cool honey quickly after heating?
options: A) Put it in the freezer
B) Place the pot in a cold water bath
C) Leave it in the sun
D) Add ice directly to the honey
quiz.explanation: A cold water bath conducts heat away rapidly without diluting the honey.

quiz.q: What is raw honey?
options: A) Honey that has been pasteurized
B) Honey that has not been heated above hive temperature
D) Honey that has been boiled
quiz.explanation: Raw honey is unheated, preserving natural enzymes and flavor.

quiz.q: Why is raw honey often more expensive?
options: A) It is harder to produce
B) It has better flavor and health benefits
quiz.explanation: Raw honey retains more nutrients and aroma, appealing to health-conscious buyers.

quiz.q: What moisture level is safe for raw honey to prevent fermentation?
quiz.explanation: Honey with moisture below 18% is less likely to ferment.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to process raw honey?
quiz.explanation: Crush and strain extracts honey without heat, preserving raw qualities.

quiz.q: What happens if you heat honey above 80Â°C?
options: B) It rapidly loses quality and forms HMF
quiz.explanation: High heat destroys enzymes and creates harmful HMF.

quiz.q: Why should you stir honey while heating?
options: B) To distribute heat evenly and avoid hot spots
quiz.explanation: Stirring prevents localized overheating that can scorch the honey.

quiz.q: What is HMF?
options: B) A chemical formed when honey is overheated
quiz.explanation: Hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) increases with overheating and indicates quality loss.

quiz.q: How long should you hold honey at 65Â°C for pasteurization?
quiz.explanation: At 65Â°C, a hold time of 15â20 minutes is effective for pasteurization.

quiz.q: What is a heat diffuser used for?
options: B) To spread heat evenly and prevent scorching
quiz.explanation: A diffuser sits between the fire and pot, distributing heat to avoid hot spots.

quiz.q: Why should you not bottle honey while it is hot?
options: A) It may shrink lids and create weak seals
quiz.explanation: Hot honey can warp lids, leading to poor seals and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a sign of fermentation in honey?
options: B) Bubbles, alcohol smell, and sour taste
quiz.explanation: Fermentation produces gas, alcohol, and sour flavors.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended temperature for decrystallizing honey?
quiz.explanation: 40â45Â°C gently melts crystals without damaging honey.

quiz.q: Why is raw honey not recommended for infants under one year?
options: B) It may contain botulism spores
quiz.explanation: Raw honey can contain Clostridium botulinum spores, dangerous for infants.

quiz.q: What equipment can help cool honey faster?
quiz.explanation: A cooling coil immersed in honey rapidly conducts heat away.

quiz.q: What should you do if you accidentally overheat a batch of honey?
options: A) Mix it with good honey
C) Use it for baking or lower-grade products
quiz.explanation: Overheated honey is lower quality but can still be used in cooking.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for honey to avoid fermentation?
quiz.explanation: Low moisture inhibits yeast growth and fermentation.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a reason to heat honey?
options: D) To make it easier to bottle
quiz.explanation: Heating reduces moisture, not increases it.

quiz.q: What is the best way to test if honey is fully capped for raw processing?
options: B) Look for white wax caps covering the cells
quiz.explanation: Fully capped combs indicate low moisture and ripe honey.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid getting water into honey during heating?
options: A) It makes honey too sweet
B) It increases moisture and can cause fermentation
quiz.explanation: Added water raises moisture content, risking fermentation.

quiz.q: What is a practical alternative to a double boiler for small batches?
quiz.explanation: Two stacked saucepans can serve as a makeshift double boiler.

quiz.q: After heating and cooling honey, what should you do before bottling?
options: B) Skim off foam and let it settle
quiz.explanation: Settling and skimming remove air bubbles and debris for clearer honey.
